tagline: A former gravel road connects forest, sandstone gorges and caves.
intro: The Hocking Hills Scenic Byway follows State Route 374 through the hills and around Hocking State Forest. Blackhand sandstone forms the region’s high cliffs and narrow, deep gorges. Ohio’s transportation department includes Hocking Hills among America’s Byways and highlights its deep gorges and caves. The forest landscape includes steep ridges, narrow valleys and exposed sandstone, with eastern hemlock among its native trees. Rock shelters and waterfalls are part of the terrain the road serves.

The numbered highway began with an unnumbered gravel road added to the state system in 1932; by 1934 it was SR 374. Extensions in 1938 carried it to SR 56 in the south and US 33 at Rockbridge in the north. During the same decade as the highway’s early expansion, Civilian Conservation Corps crews replanted trees and built trails in the forest. A later change addressed the meeting of cars and walkers: a one-mile realignment near Old Man’s Cave opened by January 2013 to reduce conflicts with pedestrians.

Traveling south, begin near Rockbridge at US 33 and follow SR 374 through the state forest and state park to SR 56, east of South Bloomingville. The park’s separate hiking areas include Rock House, Old Man’s Cave and Ash Cave, with sandstone formations reached from trails.

moments.title: Rock House
moments.text: Seven openings look past stone columns into the forest at Rock House, the only non-recess cave in Hocking Hills State Park. Indigenous people used the cave for thousands of years. Tourism followed with the construction of the Rock House Hotel in 1835. During the Depression, Civilian Conservation Corps Company 526, based at Camp Logan and largely employing Black workers, improved Rock House along with Cantwell Cliffs and Rockbridge. By the camp’s closure in 1937, Company 526 had also paved miles of roadways and planted 300,000 trees across its work areas.
moments.notice: Look through the row of seven openings past the stone columns toward the forest.

moments.title: Conkle's Hollow
moments.text: Conkle’s Hollow narrows to 100 feet in places, with cliffs about 200 feet tall above the gorge. Ferns, hemlock and wildflowers cover its floor. Two trails follow different levels of the hollow: one traces the rim, while the other follows the bottom. Nearby, the preserved main cabin of Camp Hocking marks a Civilian Conservation Corps base. Company 505 worked from this camp on erosion control, trails and stone masonry elsewhere in the Hocking Hills. Company 505’s projects included Ash Cave and Old Man’s Cave, linking the nearby camp to the trail network beyond this narrow gorge.

moments.title: Ash Cave
moments.text: Ash Cave is a recess worn into sandstone, stretching 700 feet from end to end and rising 90 feet at its highest point. Across the park, groundwater and streams eroded the sandstone over millions of years, producing the rock formations and waterfalls. Its name comes from piles of ash that white settlers found on the floor. Archaeologists believe the ashes came from campfires accumulated over centuries of use by Indigenous cultures. The space has also hosted meetings and worship services, followed by annual summer concerts by the Columbus Symphony Orchestra beginning in 2022.
